claims.text: High-entropy nanoparticles are composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The initial nanoparticles are single-phase solid solutions with homogeneous elemental distributions.
Elevated-temperature solid-solution stability is governed by competition between configurational-entropy stabilization and differential atomic mobility.
Configurational entropy, together with high diffusion barriers and sluggish kinetics, can kinetically preserve a uniform elemental distribution during annealing.
Individual constituent elements can have substantially different intrinsic diffusion barriers.
Elements with relatively low diffusion barriers become mobile under thermal activation and preferentially segregate.
If all constituent elements have comparably high diffusion barriers, entropy-driven stabilization will prevail.
Atomic mobility at elevated temperature is determined by the diffusion barrier of each element.
More mobile elements migrate to energetically favorable sites, causing segregation or clustering.
Fully diffusion-equilibrated multielement nanoparticles can exhibit clear elemental segregation.
Nanoparticles whose constituent elements all have high or similar diffusion barriers will remain single-phase throughout 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles containing elements with significantly lower diffusion barriers will show segregation, phase separation, or clustering at higher temperatures relative to their initial state.
Atmosphere, pressure, heating rate, and extraneous chemical reactions can influence nanoparticle phase behavior.
Subtle compositional variations may alter the balance between kinetic barriers and thermodynamic driving forces.
The diffusion-barrier disparity required to trigger segregation has not been quantitatively defined.

A lack of measurable segregation or phase transformation up to 1923 K in low-barrier-element samples, with behavior indistinguishable from the high-barrier comparator, would falsify the proposed governing role of differential mobility.
